400.title: The person; the gods enter through the doors of the body (1.2)
400.hook: the gods are offered a cow, then a horse, as a home, and turn both down. then they see a human being
400.tomorrow: hunger and thirst ask for a place
400.howItsDone: In Vedic and later Hindu ritual, the body's senses are linked to deities, and some rites include touching the limbs while reciting mantras, a practice called nyasa, which echoes the idea of the gods dwelling in the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday: in the beginning, the self alone, atma, which looked and said, let me create worlds. Your line was the worlds. Did you notice a small world start with a look and a wish? Day four hundred.

Day four hundred, and the Aitareya has a house-hunting story for you. The worlds are made. The self shapes a cosmic person and draws the great powers out of it: fire, wind, the sun, the moon. Gods. But the gods have nowhere to live. They're adrift, the text says, fallen into a great ocean. And they come back with a request: give us a home. So the self brings them a cow. The gods look it over and say, no, this isn't enough for us. It brings them a horse. Not enough either. Then it brings them a human being.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE NOWHERE TO LIVE.` → `A COW? NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HORSE? NOT ENOUGH.` → `THEN, A PERSON.`

segments.voice: When the gods see the person, purusha, they say: sukritam bata. Well made, indeed! The text adds: the person is truly well made. That's the Upanishad's verdict on the human body. Not a prison. Not a burden. A good piece of work, the house the gods accepted. Then the self says: enter, each into your own place. And no god just walks in. Each one changes shape to fit. Fire becomes speech, and enters the mouth. Wind becomes breath, and enters the nostrils. The sun becomes sight, and enters the eyes. The directions of space become hearing, and enter the ears. Plants and trees become the hairs, and enter the skin. The moon becomes mind, and enters the heart. Death becomes the down-going breath, and enters the navel. The waters become seed, and enter the organ of generation. Read that list slowly and the body looks different. On this map, when you talk, there's fire in your mouth. When you look up, the sun is looking out through you. Your quiet, changeable mind is the moon. Even death has a room in the house, low down, at the navel, doing its work. The Upanishad isn't asking you to worship your eyes. It's saying the great powers out there and the small doors in here belong to one system. The person is where they meet. Perhaps that's why, in the story, a cow wasn't enough, and a horse wasn't enough. They needed a place where speech, sight, mind and the rest could all live together.
screen: `WELL MADE, INDEED!` · `ENTER, EACH INTO YOUR PLACE.` · `FIRE TO SPEECH, SUN TO SIGHT.` · `THE MOON BECOMES MIND, IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `SUKRITAM BATA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes touring the doors. Sit, and bring attention to the mouth, resting closed: in the story, fire lives here, as speech. Then the nostrils, the breath moving: the wind. The eyes, closed or soft: the sun. The ears, taking in whatever sound is near: the directions. The skin, the air on it: the plants and trees. The chest, the heart: the moon, as mind. Then rest in the whole house at once, every door open. The bell holds the time.
The person. Purusha, the human being the gods called well made, the one house where fire, wind, sun and moon could each find their door.
Your line: the gods within. Today, the next time you speak, remember the story's fire in your mouth, and let it be worth the house. Day four hundred.

401.title: Hunger and thirst ask for a place (1.2)
401.hook: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
401.tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head
401.howItsDone: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the person, the house the gods called well made. Your line was the gods within. Did you speak today as if there were fire in your mouth? Day four hundred one.

Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming. And then there's a knock. Two figures are standing outside, and they've been there since before the gods arrived. In fact, they're the reason the gods went house-hunting at all. Their names are hunger and thirst. And they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. These two are easy to recognize. They turn up mid-afternoon, at midnight in front of the fridge, in long meetings. The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS FULL.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?`

segments.voice: Here's the order in the story. Back when the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat. So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan. Now, with the gods settled, the two of them ask: find a place for us. And the self doesn't banish them. It doesn't scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods. You'll be partners with them. And the text explains what that means. That's why, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. It's an ordinary arrangement, and a generous one. One way to hear it: when your eyes see, they get hungry for more seeing. When your ears hear a song, they want the next one. When the mind, the moon in the heart, settles on an idea, it gets thirsty for another. On this reading, every power comes with an appetite. The story doesn't call that a flaw. It gives hunger and thirst a home, right alongside fire and sun. Some later teachers read this passage as a sober account of the human condition: wanting runs through every sense. But the story itself is calm about it. In the story, nobody is shamed for being hungry. The self knows who lives in the house, and gives each one its share.
screen: `HUNGER AND THIRST WERE THERE FIRST.` · `THEY ASK: FIND US A PLACE.` · `A SHARE IN EVERY GOD'S OFFERING.` · `EVERY POWER COMES WITH AN APPETITE.` · then, large: `THEY TOO NEED A HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your appetites. Sit, and check: is there hunger, even a little? Thirst? Some other wanting, for your phone, for news, for this to be over? Whatever's there, don't obey it and don't fight it. Just find where it lives in the body. The stomach. The throat. The hands. Let it have that small place, the way the story does. Notice that it can sit there, known and given room, without running the house. The bell holds the time.
Appetite, the hunger and thirst that ask the self for a place. In the Aitareya, they're given no room of their own, but a share in whatever is offered to every god.
Your line: they too need a home. Today, when a craving shows up, instead of scolding it, name it and give it a seat: you're hunger, I know you. Day four hundred one.

402.title: The self enters through the crown of the head (1.3)
402.hook: the house is full of gods, and the self asks a strange question: if all of them do all the work, then who am I?
402.howItsDone: Some Hindu men, especially in priestly families, keep a tuft of hair, the shikha, near the crown, and some yoga and meditation teachers direct attention to the crown of the head, which later texts call the brahmarandhra.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hunger and thirst, appetite, given a share in every god. Your line was they too need a home. Did a craving get a seat instead of a scolding? Day four hundred two.

Here's a company where every department runs perfectly. Speech handles the talking. Breath handles the breathing. The eyes do the seeing, the ears the hearing, the mind the thinking. Reports come in, things get done. And the founder walks through the building and has an uncomfortable thought: if they all do everything, what am I for? That's where the Aitareya's first chapter ends. The self has made worlds, a person, a house full of gods and appetites. And now it looks at all that working machinery and asks how it can possibly be there without itself.
screen: `EVERY DEPARTMENT RUNS ITSELF.` → `WHAT AM I FOR?` → `THE SELF ASKS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The text gives the self two questions. First: how could this be without me? And then: by which way shall I enter? Then comes a list, almost comic. If speaking is done by speech, breathing by breath, seeing by the eye, hearing by the ear, touching by the skin, thinking by the mind, then who am I? So the self finds its own door. Not the mouth, not the nostrils, not the eyes. Those were taken. It splits open the seam at the very top of the skull, the line where the bones meet, and enters there. The text names that door vidriti, the cleft, and calls it the place of joy. Every other god came in through a working opening. The self comes in through a door that does nothing at all. It doesn't speak, see or breathe. It's just the way in. Then the text says the self has three dwelling places, three states of dream, and repeats: this is a dwelling, this is a dwelling, this is a dwelling. Commentators argue over which three. Once inside, the self looks around at everything, wondering, is there anything here that could speak of something other than me? And it sees this very person as Brahman, spread out everywhere. Idam adarsham, it says. I have seen this. Later yoga traditions talk about a point at the crown called the brahmarandhra, and some readers connect it to this passage. The Aitareya itself just says: there's a door at the top, and that's where the one who sees came in.
screen: `IF THEY DO EVERYTHING, WHO AM I?` · `THE SELF SPLITS THE SEAM AT THE CROWN.` · `A DOOR THAT DOES NOTHING BUT LET IN.` · `I HAVE SEEN THIS.` · then, large: `VIDRITI.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the door at the top. Sit tall, and let your attention rest on the crown of your head, the very top, where the seams of the skull meet. Feel whatever's there: air, warmth, the weight of your hair, or nothing much. Notice that this spot isn't doing anything. It isn't talking or watching or breathing. And still, something is aware of it. Rest in that awareness, the one that came in by the quiet door. The bell holds the time.
Vidriti, the cleft at the crown of the head where the self enters. In the Aitareya, after every god has its door, the self comes in through this door, and sees.
Your line: the door at the top. Today, when you're busy doing, talking, scrolling, pause once and ask the Aitareya's question: and who is noticing all this? Day four hundred two.

403.title: The three births — conception, birth, and death as birth (2.1)
403.hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying
403.howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the self enters through the crown of the head, vidriti. Your line was the door at the top. Did you pause once and ask who was noticing? Day four hundred three.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. But ask a family and the answer gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families, there's a day that comes after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya Upanishad's second chapter counts births too. It doesn't count from the hospital. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, like a part of her own body, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and in caring for the child, the text says, he cares for himself, for so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old, and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Death isn't the opposite of birth here. It's the next one. Then the chapter turns to a seer. It quotes a verse from the Rig Veda in the voice of the sage Vamadeva: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. The text says Vamadeva, knowing this, rose up from the body and reached immortality. Notice what the chapter honors along the way. The mother is to be nourished. Even in a list of births, it stops to say who needs care.
screen: `THE FIRST BIRTH: IN THE FATHER.` · `THE SECOND: FROM THE MOTHER.` · `THE THIRD: DEPARTING, BORN AGAIN.` · `VAMADEVA, BREAKING OUT LIKE A HAWK.` · then, large: `THREE BIRTHS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the three births. Sit, and think first of the people who carried you before you were born: a mother, a father, whoever held the hope of you. Let one breath be for them. Then think of the day you arrived, the people who fed and held you before you could thank them. Let a breath be for them. Then, gently, think of someone who has died. In the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.

Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.
Your line: three births. Today, thank someone who cared for you before you could ask, a parent, a grandparent, anyone who carried you. Day four hundred three.

404.title: "Consciousness is Brahman" — prajnanam brahma (3.1)
404.hook: the Aitareya ends by asking which one is the self, and answers with two words that became one of the great sayings
404.tomorrow: six students, one year of practice before asking
404.howItsDone: In the Advaita tradition, the four great sayings are taught to students and to those taking monastic vows, and prajnanam brahma is the one associated with the Rig Veda; teachers in other Vedanta schools comment on the same line differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the three births, Vamadeva, in the father, from the mother, and in departing. Did you thank someone who carried you before you could ask? Today, the Aitareya's last chapter. Day four hundred four.

Try this. Point at yourself. Where did your finger go? Probably the chest, maybe the face. Now ask: is that me, or is that where I keep the thing that's me? It's a children's puzzle, and a very old one. The Aitareya Upanishad saves it for its very last chapter. It has told the story of the worlds, the gods moving into the body, hunger and thirst, the door at the crown, the three births. Now it stops telling stories and asks straight out: who is this one we call the self? Which one is it? And it ends with two words.
screen: `POINT AT YOURSELF.` → `IS THAT ME?` → `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?`

segments.voice: First the question: is the self the one by which we see? By which we hear, smell, speak, taste? Then the text looks at the heart and mind and makes a long list of what they do. Awareness. Perception. Discernment. Intelligence. Wisdom. Insight. Steadiness. Thought. Reflection. Drive. Memory. Intention. Purpose. Life. Desire. Will. And then it says: all of these are only names of prajnana. Prajnana means knowing, awareness, consciousness. Pra, forth or fully, and jnana, knowing. Then the list widens. This is Brahman. This is Indra, and Prajapati, and all the gods. The five elements, earth, wind, space, water and fire. Every creature, born from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, from a sprout. Horses, cows, people, elephants, whatever breathes, walks, flies or stands still. All of it is guided by consciousness, rests on consciousness. The world has consciousness for its eye. And then: prajnanam brahma. Consciousness is Brahman. Many Hindu teachers, in the Advaita tradition, count this among four mahavakyas, great sayings, one from each Veda. This is the Rig Veda's. You've already heard the other three this year: tat tvam asi in the Chandogya, and aham brahma asmi and ayam atma brahma in the Brihadaranyaka. Schools read the saying differently. Advaita hears a strict identity: awareness and Brahman are one. Other Vedanta schools hear Brahman as the conscious ground on which all knowing depends, while keeping a distinction between the soul and God. Either way, the text is pointing somewhere specific: not at the finger, but at what's aware of it.
screen: `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?` · `ALL THESE ARE NAMES OF PRAJNANA.` · `EVERYTHING RESTS ON CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `ONE OF FOUR GREAT SAYINGS.` · then, large: `PRAJNANAM BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the Aitareya's list. Sit, and notice seeing, even with your eyes closed: light, shapes. Then hearing. Then a thought, passing. A memory. A small want. Each time, don't follow the thing itself. Notice the knowing of it. Seeing, known. Sound, known. Thought, known. If you'd like, rest in the knowing itself, which doesn't need anything to hold. The bell holds the time.
Prajnana, knowing, awareness, consciousness. Prajnanam brahma: consciousness is Brahman, the Aitareya's closing word and, in the Advaita tradition, the great saying of the Rig Veda.
Your line: the great saying. Today, once, in the middle of something ordinary, notice not the thing, but the knowing of it. Day four hundred four.

405.title: Six students, one year of practice before asking (1.1)
405.hook: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
405.tomorrow: Q1: where do creatures come from?
405.howItsDone: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; some Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: consciousness is Brahman, prajnana, prajnanam brahma, the great saying that closed the Aitareya. Did you notice the knowing of something ordinary? Today, a new Upanishad, and six people with questions. Day four hundred five.

You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You've waited months. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year. Type the question, get the answer, scroll on. The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he says to them. Prashna means question. The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.
screen: `YOUR LIST OF QUESTIONS, READY.` → `COME BACK IN A YEAR.` → `PRASHNA MEANS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Tradition places the Prashna in the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha Bharadvaja. Satyakama Shaibya. Gargya Sauryayani. Kausalya Ashvalayana. Bhargava of Vidarbha. And Kabandhi Katyayana. The text says they were devoted to Brahman, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel in hand, sure he could tell them everything. Pippalada says: stay here one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like. And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers. He promises honesty. Think about what the year does. A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex. A question carried for a year, through practice, through ordinary days, has had time to become real. Some questions answer themselves. Some change shape. And the ones still standing are worth a teacher's time. Notice, too, the three things he asks for. Not cleverness. Not money. Discipline, a steady life, and trust. In the coming days, each student asks one question. The first five: where creatures come from, which powers hold up the body, where breath comes from, what's awake in sleep, and what happens to the one who meditates on om.
screen: `SIX STUDENTS, FUEL IN HAND.` · `STAY ONE MORE YEAR.` · `IF WE KNOW, WE'LL TELL YOU.` · `A QUESTION CARRIED BECOMES REAL.` · then, large: `EARN THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of waiting, the way Pippalada's students waited. Sit, and let the body settle. When the urge comes to move, check something, or get on with the day, notice it and stay. That's a small tapas. Keep it simple: one breath, then the next. And trust the bell to keep the time, so you don't have to. If a question rises, let it stand at the door, fuel in hand, until later. The bell holds the time.
Six students. The seekers of the Prashna Upanishad, told by the sage Pippalada to live a year in discipline and faith before asking, and promised only: if we know, we'll tell you.
Your line: earn the question. Today, before you search for the answer to something, carry the question a little longer, and see if it changes. Day four hundred five.

screen: `DAY 405 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?`

406.title: Q1: where do creatures come from? matter and breath (1)
406.hook: the first student asks where living things come from, and Pippalada answers with a pair: matter and breath, moon and sun
406.carry: the two paths of the sun
406.tomorrow: Q2: which gods hold the body?
406.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the sun's northward turn at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and treat the northern half of the year, uttarayana, as an auspicious time, an idea that echoes the two paths of texts like this one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six students, told to wait a year. Your line was earn the question. Did you carry a question a little longer before searching? The year is up. Day four hundred six, the end of week fifty-eight.

A year has passed. The six students have kept the discipline. And the first to step forward is Kabandhi Katyayana, with a question as old as asking. Sir, he says, from where are these creatures born? Children ask some version of it. Where did I come from? Where did the dog come from, the ants, the trees? A biologist would answer one way. A grandmother might answer another. Pippalada answers with a story, and at the center of the story is a pair, two things that need each other, the way a song needs both silence and sound.
screen: `THE YEAR IS UP.` → `SIR, WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?` → `THE ANSWER IS A PAIR.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, wanted offspring. He did tapas, the inner heat you met with Bhrigu. And from that heat he produced a pair: rayi and prana. Rayi means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form. Prana is breath, life, the energy that moves it. These two together, he thought, will make creatures for me. Then the pair shows up everywhere. The sun is prana. The moon is rayi. In a month, the dark half belongs to rayi, the bright half to prana. In a day, night is rayi, day is prana. Food, too, is Prajapati, because from food comes the seed from which creatures are born. Matter and life, always in pairs. Then the answer turns to people. The year itself, Pippalada says, is Prajapati, and it has two paths, a southern and a northern. Those who honor sacrifice and good works, digging wells, giving, keeping the rites, take the southern path, the path of the ancestors, to the world of the moon. And from there they return. Those who seek the self through tapas, a disciplined life, faith and knowledge, take the northern path, to the sun. That, the text says, is the resting place of breath, the immortal, the fearless. From there they do not return. So where do creatures come from? From matter meeting breath. And where do they go? The text names two paths, and what sets a person on either one is how they live.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TAPAS MAKES A PAIR.` · `RAYI IS MATTER; PRANA IS BREATH.` · `THE MOON AND THE SUN.` · `TWO PATHS: SOUTHERN AND NORTHERN.` · then, large: `RAYI AND PRANA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the pair. Sit, and feel the body's weight: bones, muscle, the pressure where you touch the chair or floor. That's rayi, matter, the moon side. Then feel the breath moving through it, warming it, lifting it. That's prana, the sun side. Let your attention rest on both at once: the stillness that holds and the motion that lives. Neither one is enough alone. The bell holds the time.
Rayi, wealth and matter, paired with prana, breath. Where do creatures come from? From rayi and prana, the moon and the sun, which Prajapati made as a pair.

Your line: the two paths of the sun. Today, notice your good works and your inner work, and give each one a few minutes. And that's week fifty-eight: the person, hunger and thirst, the door at the top, three births, the great saying, six students, and matter and breath. Day four hundred six.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-EIGHT: THE PERSON · HUNGER · THE CROWN · THREE BIRTHS · PRAJNANA · SIX STUDENTS · Q1`

original.note: Sanskrit rayi: wealth, substance, matter. paired with prāṇa, breath, in Prashna 1.4.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sun and moon are just sky decorations in old texts.
what it means: in the Prashna, the sun is breath and the moon is matter, and the year has two paths, one that returns and one that doesn't.
what a scholar hears: the southern path of the ancestors (pitryāna) and the northern path of the gods (devayāna) of Prashna 1.9–10 also appear in the Chandogya, Brihadaranyaka and Gita 8.24–25.
